articles.title: COVID-19 vaccination and non-pharmaceutical interventions in selected European settings: a systematic review.
articles.summary: PMID: 43025126. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129337. BackgroundCOVID-19 pandemic responses in European countries relied on both vaccination campaigns and non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs). While vaccination reduced severe disease, NPIs remained necessary to limit transmission, particularly during periods of variant emergence. However, the effectiveness of these strategies depended on social trust, communication clarity, and behavioural adaptation.ObjectiveTo synthesize empirical evidence on shared determinants of vaccination and NPI-related behaviours, behavioural relationships between these strategies, and evidence concerning their joint epidemiological effects.MethodsPubMed and Scopus were searched on 11 February 2025 using free-text terms for COVID-19, vaccination, and social or non-pharmaceutical measures. Eligible studies were peer-reviewed, empirical (quantitative, qualitative, or mixed-methods), conducted by authors affiliated with selected European institutions, and examined relationships between vaccination and NPIs. Studies based solely on modelling or secondary data were excluded. Data were synthesized narratively due to heterogeneity of study designs and outcomes.ResultsTwelve studies met inclusion criteria. Trust in scientific and governmental authorities consistently predicted adherence to NPIs and willingness to vaccinate. Sweden's reliance on voluntary measures was effective where institutional trust was high. In contrast, inconsistent communication in the United Kingdom contributed to reduced adherence and public frustration. Vaccinated individuals tended to increase social contacts, an association compatible with behavioural adaptation. A conjoint experiment examined stated vaccination preferences in relation to NPI attributes. Younger populations experienced notable psychological strain during prolonged restrictions.ConclusionsThe synthesis primarily informs social and behavioural relationships involving vaccination and NPIs. Shared determinants and behavioural associations should not be interpreted as evidence of synergistic effects on infection, hospitalisation, or mortality. Future pandemic preparedness should prioritize trust-building, consistent messaging, and targeted psychosocial support for vulnerable groups.

articles.title: Socio-spatial inequalities in routine childhood vaccination in Latin America and the Caribbean: a scoping review of territorial, social, and health service determinants.
articles.summary: PMID: 43033782. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129356. BackgroundRoutine childhood vaccination inequalities in Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) are shaped by social, territorial, and health-service conditions, but the evidence is dispersed across designs and scales.MethodsWe conducted a JBI-guided scoping review reported according to PRISMA-ScR. Six information sources were searched from inception through 15 August 2026 without language restrictions; the protocol was prospectively registered in OSF (10.17605/OSF.IO/ZSX6W).ResultsThe registered searches yielded 3251 records and 225 included reports; one additional eligible report was identified through other methods, giving 226 reports. Brazil contributed 126 reports (55.8%). Non-exclusive design features included cross-sectional/survey (69), ecological/administrative (49), cohort/longitudinal (21), spatial (18), qualitative (11), and explicit intervention/program-evaluation designs (9). Twenty-eight reports explicitly examined pandemic-related disruption or recovery. Socioeconomic gradients were not consistently monotonic, and direct Caribbean evidence was sparse.ConclusionsThe literature maps substantial socio-spatial heterogeneity in childhood vaccination but does not support a single causal hierarchy of determinants. More geographically balanced research using explicit equity stratification and evaluative designs is needed.

articles.title: Estimating the global and regional impact of introducing typhoid conjugate vaccination schedules: a modelling study.
articles.summary: PMID: 43044464. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129352. BackgroundIn 2018, WHO recommended single-dose typhoid conjugate vaccines (TCVs) for typhoid-endemic countries. Emerging evidence of waning immunity has raised questions about optimal vaccination age and booster doses. A follow-up multi-model study evaluated vaccination schedules, focusing on booster strategies. Here, we expand findings from one of four modelling groups, estimating the global and regional health impact of TCV schedules.MethodologyWe developed an agent-based typhoid transmission model using the open-source Starsim toolbox. The model captures subclinical and acute infections, chronic carriers, and natural and vaccine-derived immunity, with age- and sex-specific parameters and outcomes. The model was calibrated to three incidence archetypes (medium, high, and very high) and two vaccine-derived immunity durations (fast and slow waning). Countries were mapped to archetypes based on national typhoid burden. We compared no vaccination with four strategies: routine vaccination at 9 months, 9 months with a booster at 5 years, 2 years, and 5 years, each with a catch-up campaign. Cases, deaths, and DALYs averted were estimated globally and across GBD super-regions over 10 years.ResultsGlobally, up to 29.5 million cases and 8.2 million DALYs could be averted with routine vaccination at 9 months plus a 5-year booster. Earlier vaccination and longer-lasting immunity generally increased impact. Under fast waning, vaccination at 2 years averted more cases and DALYs than vaccination at 9 months or 5 years, particularly in high-incidence settings where burden was greatest among children aged 2-<5 years. Boosters provided additional benefits, especially with fast waning. South Asia accounted for the largest share of global impact, followed by Sub-Saharan Africa.ConclusionTCV could avert substantial typhoid burden. The optimal age for a single dose depends on how quickly protection wanes, and boosters add benefit where waning is rapid. Better evidence on the protection duration, and country-specific analyses, are needed to guide schedule choices.

articles.title: Pneumococcal vaccination coverage among adults aged 18-64 years at risk and aged ≥65 years in the United States - behavioral risk factor surveillance system 2024.
articles.summary: PMID: 43033783. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129355. IntroductionPneumococcal disease, including invasive disease and non-bacteremic pneumonia, causes substantial morbidity among older U.S. adults and those with certain underlying medical conditions. We assessed pneumococcal vaccination and associated factors among adults aged 18-64 years with pneumococcal risk conditions and adults aged ≥65 years using 2024 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) data.MethodsWe conducted a cross-sectional analysis. Adults aged 18-64 years were classified as having risk conditions if they reported ≥1 prespecified pneumococcal risk condition or current/former smoking. The primary outcome was self-reported lifetime receipt of any pneumococcal vaccine; BRFSS did not collect product, dose, timing, or complete vaccination history. Weighted coverage estimates and adjusted prevalence ratios were calculated by sociodemographic and access-to-care characteristics.ResultsCoverage was 34.1% among adults aged 18-64 years with risk conditions and 70.3% among adults aged ≥65 years. Among adults aged ≥65 years, coverage was higher for those with risk conditions (74.6%) than for those without (63.4%) (p < 0.05). Coverage was 50.1% among all adults aged ≥50 years. In adjusted analyses, coverage was lower among Hispanic adults aged 18-64 years with risk conditions and non-Hispanic Black adults aged ≥65 years than among respective non-Hispanic White adults.ConclusionsSelf-reported receipt of any pneumococcal vaccine was 34.1% among adults <65 years with risk conditions and 70.3% among all adults aged ≥65 years. Improving healthcare access and engagement may improve vaccination. These estimates provide a baseline for evaluating expanded recommendations for all adults aged ≥50 years issued in late 2024 but do not represent current recommendation-concordant coverage.

articles.title: School-based measles vaccination screening and catch-up program implementation in Zambia: costing study.
articles.summary: PMID: 43033784. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129334. Many children in Zambia miss measles vaccination through routine immunization, while supplementary immunization activities (SIAs) targeting children under five may not reach older under-vaccinated children. School-based vaccination screening and catch-up (SVS) is a recommended strategy to identify and vaccinate these children, but evidence on its implementation and cost in sub-Saharan Africa is limited. We estimated the cost of an SVS pilot for measles vaccination in Zambia to inform implementation and potential scale-up. We conducted an ingredients-based costing from the Government of Zambia perspective of an SVS pilot in 20 urban schools in Lusaka and rural schools in Masaiti. Costs were estimated under three scenarios: base case (full pilot costs); post-introduction (excluding start-up and technical support); and budgeting (assuming full program integration and excluding start-up, technical support, and Ministry of Health and Education staff costs). One-way and probabilistic sensitivity analyses were conducted. Costs are reported in 2024 USD and Zambian kwacha (ZMW). Among 3351 children screened, 215 were identified as measles-rubella (MR) zero-dose and 211 were vaccinated. Total implementation cost was USD 75,886 (ZMW 2,111,157) in the base case. By input, personnel accounted for 70.6% of costs. By SVS activity, coordination and training accounted for 46.8% and 34.0% of total costs, respectively. Costs decreased by 28.3% in the post-introduction and 42.4% in the budgeting scenario. Cost per child screened was USD 13.05-22.65, and cost per MR zero-dose child vaccinated was USD 208.29-360.70. Coordination time was the most influential parameter. While costs per child are relatively high, SVS is a targeted strategy that can be used to reach older children who remain unreached by routine immunization programs and SIAs. Efficiency could improve through streamlined documentation, integration with school health activities, and reduced coordination and personnel requirements. Further research should assess its comparative value and cost-effectiveness against other approaches.

articles.title: Targeting T follicular helper (Tfh) Cells for Improved Vaccine Efficacy: Lessons from Diverse Disease Models.
articles.summary: PMID: 43050926. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129357. Despite remarkable progress in vaccinology, many vaccines fail to generate durable and broadly protective immunity against rapidly evolving and deadly pathogens. Conventional vaccine strategies often rely on quantifying antibody titers or neutralizing antibodies, but accumulating evidence suggests that humoral responses alone may not ensure long-term protection. An effective vaccine must engage multiple components of the immune system, harnessing intricate cellular interactions to generate durable immunological memory. Among these, CD4+ T follicular helper (Tfh) cells have emerged as central players in orchestrating germinal center (GC) dynamics, where they provide essential signals to B cells for affinity maturation, class switching, and differentiation into memory B cells and long-lived plasma cells. Tfh cells thus directly shape the magnitude and quality of vaccine-induced antibody responses. Clinical and experimental studies across infections such as influenza, HIV, HBV, and SARS-CoV-2 highlight that robust Tfh responses correlate with effective immunity and reduced disease severity. However, most licensed vaccines elicit suboptimal or short-lived Tfh activation, underscoring a critical limitation in current vaccine design. This review provides a comprehensive overview of vaccines targeting Tfh cells across various diseases, elucidating their mechanistic contributions to vaccine-induced immunity, and how their modulation could improve next-generation vaccine strategies. By harnessing Tfh biology, future vaccines could achieve durable, high-quality antibody responses, offering improved protection against emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases.

articles.title: A next generation vaccine to prevent disease caused by Neisseria meningitidis serogroup B (MenB).
articles.summary: PMID: 43044465. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129354. BackgroundOMVax has developed a meningococcal native outer membrane vesicle (NOMV) vaccine containing overexpressed, mutant Factor H binding proteins (FHbps) from subfamilies A and B with reduced FH binding and attenuated endotoxin (NOMV-FHbp). In previous studies, NOMV presented surface antigens in a native environment that elicited high titers of serum bactericidal activity (SBA) in mice and infant macaques. However, the relatively low amounts of NOMV produced by MenB strains has limited vaccine development.MethodsWe describe here a culture medium enabling commercial scale production of NOMV. We investigated the ability of antibodies elicited in mice by NOMV-FHbp alone or in combination with a MenACWY capsular polysaccharide conjugate vaccine to elicit human complement-mediated serum bactericidal activity (SBA) against strains from each capsular group.ResultsIn CD1 wild-type (WT) mice, anti-NOMV-FHbp antibodies showed significantly greater SBA than those elicited by marketed MenB vaccine MenB-FHbp against five out of six representative MenB strains currently causing disease. The combination NOMV-FHbp+MenACWY vaccine maintained high SBA activity against strains from the different serogroups compared to each individual vaccine. In CEACAM1/FH human transgenic mice, anti-NOMV-FHbp antibodies showed greater or comparable SBA than those elicited by MenB-4C licensed vaccine against two MenB strains expressing FHbp ID 1, an amino acid sequence identical to FHbp ID 1 in the MenB-4C vaccine.ConclusionsThe results show that NOMV-FHbp alone or in combination with MenACWY vaccines has the potential to broaden protection against MenB strains that are not optimally covered by existing vaccines.

articles.title: Immunosenescence and vaccine adjuvants in older adults: from immune decline to signal reconstitution strategies.
articles.summary: PMID: 43033779. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129348. Immunosenescence is characterized by progressive deterioration of innate and adaptive immune function, resulting in reduced vaccine efficacy, durability, and immune quality in older adults. Age-associated alterations include impaired dendritic cell activation, reduced type I interferon production, diminished naïve T-cell output, defective T follicular helper cell differentiation, weakened germinal center responses, and chronic low-grade inflammation. Consequently, vaccine responsiveness in older adults is often limited by defects in immune signaling and coordination that cannot be fully overcome by antigen optimization alone. In this review, we examine the biological basis of immunosenescence and discuss how vaccine adjuvants can improve immune responses in aging populations. We propose a conceptual framework in which adjuvants act through three non-mutually exclusive mechanisms: signal amplification, signal reconstitution, and functional bypass. Using this framework, we evaluate licensed adjuvants currently used in older adults, including AS01, MF59, AS03, and CpG1018, and discuss emerging adjuvant platforms under development. Collectively, current evidence suggests that effective vaccination in older adults requires strategies that address age-associated immune dysfunction in addition to antigen delivery. A better understanding of immunosenescence and adjuvant biology may facilitate the development of precision vaccination approaches tailored to specific immune deficits in aging populations.

articles.title: Maternal respiratory syncytial virus vaccination: A systematic review and meta-analysis of determinants of vaccine acceptability and uptake.
articles.summary: PMID: 43056785. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129371. ObjectiveMaternal respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccination has potential to prevent infant respiratory morbidity. We identified sociodemographic factors influencing the acceptability and uptake of RSV vaccination among pregnant individuals.MethodsWe carried out a systematic review and meta-analysis of sociodemographic factors associated with maternal RSV vaccination behavior. We searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, and Web of Science for observational studies of RSV vaccination in pregnant women published before September 10, 2025. We included articles that examined how maternal race/ethnicity, education, employment, age, and marital status were related to RSV vaccine intention and uptake. We performed a meta-analysis using random effects models with inverse-variance weighting to estimate pooled odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for the association between sociodemographic factors and RSV vaccination intention and uptake.ResultsSeventeen studies comprising 15,275 individuals met inclusion criteria. Black race was the strongest determinant of vaccination behavior during pregnancy, followed by socioeconomic factors. In meta-analysis, Black race was associated with more than 50% lower odds of RSV vaccine uptake compared with White race (OR 0.43, 95% CI 0.32-0.57; 6 studies). Low educational attainment (OR 0.59, 95% CI 0.45-0.76; 8 studies) and unemployment (OR 0.73, 95% CI 0.56-0.96; 7 studies) were associated with >20% less intention to be vaccinated compared with higher education or employment. Maternal age and marital status were not associated with RSV vaccination intention.ConclusionBlack patients and patients from low socioeconomic backgrounds should be a primary focus of obstetric RSV vaccination efforts.

articles.title: Misperceived norms and willingness to get a COVID-19 vaccine: a whole-population study of adults in rural Uganda.
articles.summary: PMID: 43050925. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129351. BackgroundPerceptions about others' willingness to get vaccinated for COVID-19 are understudied in HIV-endemic settings. Perceived social norms influence engagement in other protective behaviors. Information about COVID-19 vaccine norms could inform future HIV vaccination efforts.MethodsAll adults across 8 villages in Uganda completed a survey in 2021-2022. Participants reported personal willingness to take a COVID-19 vaccine (definitely yes vs any hesitance) and estimated how many village adults would take a COVID-19 vaccine ("all or almost all," "more than half," "less than half," "very few or no one," "do not know"). Participants also reported COVID-19 related beliefs, whether they knew someone who had COVID-19, personal HIV status, and sociodemographic characteristics. A multivariable Poisson regression model estimated associations between perceptions about others' willingness to get a vaccine and personal willingness to get a vaccine.ResultsAmong 1561 participants (>90% response rate), 1163 (75%) were willing to get a COVID-19 vaccine. One in three vaccine-hesitant participants and 1 in 10 vaccine-willing participants incorrectly thought most adults in their village would not get vaccinated. Compared to participants who thought more than half of villagers were willing to get vaccinated, those who mistakenly thought fewer than half (adjusted relative risk [aRR] = 0.81; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.70-0.94) or few to none (aRR = 0.65; 95% CI: 0.50-0.85) were willing were less likely to report willingness themselves.ConclusionsOverall, one-fifth of adults mistakenly thought most other villagers were unwilling to get vaccinated. Adults with this misperception were less willing to get a COVID-19 vaccine themselves. Strategies that provide information about vaccine effectiveness and communicate that most adults are willing to get vaccinated may increase uptake. Changing perceived norms about vaccine uptake may also foster conversations about accessing vaccines and reduce vaccine-related stigma, important considerations with an HIV vaccine on the horizon.

articles.title: Cellular predictors of serological response to sequential pneumococcal vaccination in people living with HIV: A lymphocyte immunophenotyping study.
articles.summary: PMID: 43033780. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129344. BackgroundPeople living with HIV (PLWHA) remain at higher risk of invasive pneumococcal disease despite vaccination, and predictors of vaccine response beyond CD4+ count are poorly defined. We evaluated cellular and humoral responses to the 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV-13), followed or not by the 23-valent polysaccharide vaccine (PPV-23), in PLWHA with chronic infection, compared with HIV-negative controls, and investigated lymphocyte subpopulations as predictors of serological response.MethodsIn this prospective cohort study (Brazil, April 2023-November 2025; RBR-3qppfyq), 93 participants (PPV-23-naive, CHI-N, n = 26; PPV-23-experienced, CHI-E, n = 33; HIV-negative controls, NonHC, n = 34) received PCV-13, with or without subsequent PPV-23, and were followed for 24 months. T- and B-lymphocyte phenotypes and immunoglobulin G (IgG) against seven serotypes were analyzed with Linear Mixed Models and Spearman correlations.ResultsBoth PLWHA groups had higher frequencies of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells expressing human leukocyte antigen-DR (HLA-DR) than controls. Baseline CD8 + HLA-DR+ correlated negatively with serotype 6B response in CHI-E (r = -0.38 to -0.58). Non-switched memory B cells declined in all groups after vaccination, but only controls partially recovered at 24 months, when CHI-E values were lower than controls (p < 0.001). Seroconversion at 24 months was lower in CHI-E than in controls (38.5% vs 93.3%, adjusted p = 0.001), without differences involving CHI-N (71.4%, n = 7). The CD4/CD8 ratio was not associated with seroconversion.ConclusionsHLA-DR expression on T cells is a candidate, hypothesis-generating predictor of pneumococcal vaccine response in PLWHA. The decline of non-switched memory B cells was not restricted to PPV-23-experienced participants, and its lack of recovery requires confirmation.
